newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria Socialist congress deals blow to reformers.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria Socialist congress deals blow to reformers.

text.p: A congress of Bulgaria's ruling Socialists rejected a package of measures proposed by party reformers on Sunday, raising Prime Minister Zhan Videnov's chances of being returned to the post he quit a day earlier.
Videnov's critics met on the edges of the congress to discuss alternative candidates, but voting was not expected before early Monday.

A total of 153 reformist delegates had proposed a package of seven resolutions, including statements on economic reform, media policy, the ex-communist party's commitment to social democracy, and relations with other political parties.

Delegates used to communist-style congresses approved them automatically, but then Videnov said that one resolution implied the separation of the posts of party leader and prime minister and insisted they be voted again.
Nikolai Kamov, head of parliament's foreign policy committee, said the leadership issue was preventing the congress from considering anything else.
"The party is dead," he said. "They refused to amend the statutes and adopt a programme just because of one person."
"The delegates are now voting mechanically against the reformists," said Valentin Vatsev, a prominent party ideologue close to Videnov.

The 37-year-old premier stunned delegates by announcing at Saturday's opening session that he felt he lacked the necessary support to continue as premier and party leader and had submitted his resignation to parliament.
His critics dismissed the move as a ploy aimed at proving he had the support of his party, observing that parliament was in recess and speaker Blagovest Sendov was in Israel.
But he caught his party critics off guard, and they have been unable to agree on a candidate to replace him.

"This decision should have been taken 40 days ago when it became evident that there was no confidence in the government," said foreign minister Georgi Pirinski, who resigned last month after a party confidence vote gave Videnov only narrow backing.

Pirinski told the congress he had quit because Videnov's government did not have sufficient public support to implement a tough monetary regime proposed by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) as a last-ditch attempt to halt economic collapse.
Delegates painted a bleak picture of the country's crisis and called for a genuine commitment to reform and concrete measures to fight corruption.
"I insist on a change of policy and a change in the style of government," said Interior Minister Nikolai Dobrev, another potential rival to Videnov.
"The fight against corruption should be a main aim for this congress," he said, citing crooked insurance companies who cooperated with officials of his ministry.

Videnov became prime minister after parliamentary elections in December 1994. Criticism of his government, which is half way through its four year term, became more vocal after the Socialists' defeat in last month's presidential election.
The government's failure to meet reform targets including closing or restructuring loss-making state enterprises has led to the suspension of funding from the World Bank and IMF.

The government has not yet finalised the 1997 budget. Videnov has accepted an IMF proposal for a currency board fixed exchange rate mechanism, expected to be set up early next year to restore confidence and halt the slide in the lev.
